item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Nearly 100 US troops injured by Iran strikes, Pentagon says
item.description:
Nearly 100 US troops injured by Iran strikes, Pentagon says

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 07/21/2026 - 21:17
The disclosure came soon after the Pentagon denounced a New York Times report that said it had withheld casualty numbers
This screen grab made on 18 July 2026 from handout video footage released by the US Central Command on 17 July 2026 shows what the US military says is the latest wave of strikes (US Centcom/AFP)
Off

Nearly 100 American service members have sustained some degree of injury since 7 July, in the latest wave of fighting between the US and Iran, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on Monday.

Iran has been retaliating against nightly US strikes by targeting its military bases across Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, and Kuwait. 

The Pentagon’s disclosure came nearly five hours after spokesperson Parnell denounced a New York Times report saying that the Pentagon withheld dozens of US military injuries in the Iran war as “baseless” and “malicious” .

“This is the most transparent Department of War in history. We challenge the so-called journalists who wrote these lies, one of whom was recently subpoenaed regarding an alleged violation of federal criminal law, to stop the smears against the finest warfighting force on Earth,” Parnell said.

As early as Tuesday morning, the official Pentagon database tracking US casualties showed that no US forces were killed or wounded in action in July. 

The Department of War has now published that three US Army soldiers were killed in ballistic missile attacks on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan over the weekend: Private Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas; Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii; and a third soldier provisionally listed as missing.

In Iraq, Sergeant Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, of Fayetteville, North Carolina, was killed and another soldier was wounded over the weekend during a “controlled detonation” of an Iranian attack drone at Erbil Air Base.

Parnell said in his X post that further casualty updates would be available on the Defense Casualty Analysis System, a site tracking “deceased, wounded, ill or injured” service members for Congress and the president. He stated that a vast majority of the injured only experienced “minor concussions” and 96 percent had since returned to work.

The Pentagon has had a well-documented history of “casualty cover-up” throughout the war on Iran, according to The Intercept. 

The breakdown of the 60-day ceasefire triggered by the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding has been followed by a series of escalatory attacks by the US and Iran.

Escalation

Tehran has said it is ready to "welcome" an American ground invasion, as US Central Command (Centcom) reported its ninth consecutive night of strikes on Iran after the deaths of American soldiers in Jordan and Iraq over the weekend. 

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said that the country's leadership is “counting down the minutes to welcome” US forces in any ground invasion.

He added that the text of the Pakistan-brokered interim deal signed with the US in June is "completely clear", and that there is "no excuse" for Washington to violate the treaty.

In the early hours of Monday morning, the US military said in a post on X that its attacks hit “Iranian military command centers, air defense and coastal surveillance sites, maritime capabilities, missile and drone launch sites and communications networks”.

It added that the fresh onslaught aims to “further diminish Iran’s ability to attack commercial vessels and civilian mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz”.

US President Donald Trump said the latest round of “very hard” attacks came in “honor” of three American service members who had been killed over recent days.

“We hit them very hard again tonight, and we did that in honor of the, probably three, it's probably three great patriots," he told reporters. 

He said that Iran has "been very, very badly damaged. They've lost everything almost - militarily".

"They've got some missiles, some drones, some manufacturing ability, not much."

When asked about the military fatalities, Trump responded that "we feel very badly", adding that those who died were fighting so that Tehran "cannot have a nuclear weapon".

Also on Monday, Iranian state news media reported strikes targeting several locations in the southern port city of Bushehr, home to the country's civilian nuclear plant.

"A few minutes ago, several locations in Bushehr city were hit by [the] American enemy's projectiles," said Bushehr Governor Mohammad Mozaffari, adding that the scope and extent of the strikes are under investigation.

Tehran called on the International Atomic Energy Agency on Sunday to condemn a US attack on its Darkhovin nuclear plant, which is still under construction in the country’s southwest.

Iran's Atomic Energy Organisation denounced the attack as "a clear violation of international law".

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] 'This will be your legacy': Aoun seeks financing for Lebanon, pressure on Israel
item.description:
'This will be your legacy': Aoun seeks financing for Lebanon, pressure on Israel

Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Tue, 07/21/2026 - 18:21
In return, Trump allows US airlines to fly to Lebanon for the first time in decades
US President Donald Trump laughs while shaking hands with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun during their meeting in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, DC, on 21 July 2026 (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)
Off

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun on Tuesday largely steered clear of the potential minefield that comes with being in front of the press alongside US President Donald Trump, as the two leaders met for the very first time at the White House. 

The sit-down is a highly coveted opportunity for Aoun, who assumed office just two weeks before Trump's inauguration in January 2025. 

The last Lebanese president to sit in the Oval Office was Michel Sleiman in 2009, with former President Barack Obama. 

"Been looking forward to this visit for a very long time, meeting such a great president like yourself," Aoun said in English, prompting the US president to swiftly acknowledge the praise: "See, he knows how to get to me. Now he can have anything he wants."

What Aoun wants is a committed US engagement to Lebanon that comes with increased pressure on Israel, as well as ramped-up financing for the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) and reconstruction of the decimated south. 

What he received instead after he departed was an announcement from Trump that US airlines will now be permitted to fly directly to Lebanon - something that has not happened in 40 years.

"I am hereby directing my Administration to allow all US airline carriers to fly directly to Lebanon so that Americans can easily visit this beautiful land," he wrote on his social media platform, TruthSocial.

Flights were barred by the Ronald Reagan administration in 1985 after Hezbollah members hijacked TWA Flight 847, in a bid to demand the release of Lebanese citizens in Israeli custody. 

"It's a win [for Aoun] if it's easier for people to travel to Lebanon in a safe fashion," ‪Anthony Wanis-St John, a conflict resolution expert and professor at American University in Washington, DC, told Middle East Eye.

Safety, of course, depends on the stability of the country. And until Lebanon is no longer in open hostilities with Israel, it's unlikely to draw American tourists. 

'This will be your legacy'

Much like every other Arab leader who has been in the Oval Office over the past 18 months, Aoun is keenly aware that only Trump has the capacity and leverage to rein in Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his war on Lebanon.

"The ultimate objective [is] ending the state of hostility between Lebanon and Israel forever," Aoun told reporters.

"I think, Mr President, this will be your legacy," he said, looking at Trump.

The de facto Israeli occupation of large parts of the south since March of this year has raised the Lebanese death toll to more than 4,300 since Hezbollah began its rocket attacks on Israel on 8 October 2023, in a show of support for Palestinians in Gaza. 

Though Hezbollah has no part in any US-hosted Lebanese-Israeli negotiations, Trump acknowledged the group's critical role in moving the trilateral framework forward.

"I would speak to Hezbollah. I speak to everybody," Trump said. "If the president wanted me to speak to Hezbollah - you know he's lived with Hezbollah for a long time - if the president wanted me to speak to Hezbollah, I would."

But there is little indication Aoun would entertain the option, given his visit is meant to affirm that there is only one state authority in Lebanon.

Iraqi government orders probe over weapons smuggling to Hezbollah in Lebanon
Read More »

Hezbollah, which was born out of the Israeli occupation of Lebanon in the 1980s, has been a designated terrorist group in the US since 1997. 

Asked by a reporter about Lebanon's parliamentary speaker, Nabih Berri, cautioning that confrontations between LAF and Hezbollah fighters could lead to a Lebanese civil war, Aoun insisted that the declaration-style framework "doesn't require the endorsement of the parliament... it's part of our constitution [that] it's a prerogative of the president, and we are committed to it."

Berri, the founder of the Shia-majority Amal movement, which is aligned with Hezbollah's lawmakers, "really wants to see the end of this war", Aoun said.

"He's from the south... unfortunately, the south is being destroyed in front of his eyes. So he's actually supporting what we are doing, but we need to be careful. His position as a speaker and as a leader of the Shia community, we have to understand how critical is his position," Aoun said.

'Small step to nowhere'

US ambassador to Lebanon Michel Issa told the Lebanese broadcaster LBC last week that Aoun "won’t be leaving Washington empty-handed". 

But after a meeting that lasted just under two hours on Tuesday, Trump's senior advisor on Arab and Middle Eastern Affairs, the Lebanese businessman Massad Boulos indicated to reporters that the key deliverable is "all about implementing this agreement, which is historic".

That agreement, signed on 26 June, began implementation on Monday, with the Trump administration announcing that "pilot zone operations began in the villages of Froun, Srifa, and Zawtar Al-Gharbiya... under the auspices of the Military Coordination Group for Lebanon". 

The idea of the "pilot zones" is that as Israeli forces move out, the LAF will move in to take over the task of disarming Hezbollah.

But this is no Israeli withdrawal, as Trump pointed out on Tuesday, when he confirmed the Israeli forces are "in the process of redeploying to other sections". 

"In other words, the implication is Israel is staying on Lebanese territory," Khalil Jahshan, executive director of the Arab Center Washington DC, told MEE.

"It doesn't solve the issue of sovereignty for Lebanon. It doesn't solve the issue of foreign occupation for Lebanon," Jahshan added. "It does not offer the Lebanese government any potential to kind of go back to Hezbollah and say, 'See, it's working partially - a small area, but it's working.' So it's basically a small step to nowhere."

Wanis-St John said while Hezbollah is "losing popularity" on its own accord among the Lebanese because of the high cost of death and displacement, "the Israelis go and make them more popular by staying and being extremely violent". 

When asked by reporters what leverage Washington has over Hezbollah, Boulos responded: “There are always options."

"You have seen already some of them by the Treasury Department," he added, in reference to the spate of sanctions the US has levied on entities believed to be materially supporting the group. 

"It’s going to take time," Boulos said. "This is not easy. Nobody believes for a second that this is going to be an easy task in any way,” Boulos said. "But we are determined - President Trump is absolutely determined - to see this through. He is the president of peace, as we all know."

Election on the horizon

Aaron David Miller, a former US negotiator on Middle East issues for both Republican and Democratic administrations, said on X on Sunday that unless Aoun can extract a Trump commitment for a "a massive increase in training, weapons and intelligence for LAF", anything less would be "performative". 

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Washington is considering vetting and training units of elite fighters from the LAF specifically to take on Hezbollah's soldiers, who are thus far the more entrenched and better-equipped side. 

Netanyahu claims Israel protects Christians after Israeli attacks hit churches in Lebanon
Read More »

Jahshan suggested that the more likely strategy for the Americans is a waiting game.

"What the US is trying to do is keep the process alive somehow until the Israeli elections take place, and there is a government - this government or a new one - that can deliver," he told MEE. "In the interim, Lebanon has no choice under its current leadership but to put up with [what are] essentially promises. Undeliverable promises."

Wanis-St John agreed.

"This is definitely tied to Israeli political and electoral cycles," he told MEE. 

Legislative elections are set to take place in Israel at the end of October.

Boulos, however, rebuffed the notion that the two issues are related when pressed by reporters.

"There is no direct link. The agreement is an agreement that is going to be implemented step by step. It’s not a question of specific dates that are cast in stone,” he said. “There is a verification mechanism. We have to give it a chance. It has to work and it’s going to work."

Moments before Boulos stepped outside to defend the administration's plans, he had been standing in the Oval Office watching Trump and Aoun take questions. The US president frequently referred to having "friends in Lebanon" and even made reference to his Turkey, Syria, and Iraq envoy, Tom Barrack, as being of Lebanese descent. 

Barrack, however, was not in the room. And even though Aoun quietly gestured to Boulos, Trump failed to acknowledge his presence or that Boulos is part of the Trump family.

His son Michael is married to Trump's youngest daughter, Tiffany.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Lack of defibrillators could put 16m at risk of death by cardiac arrest in England and Wales
item.description:
Exclusive: Research shows millions live more than a 1km round trip from 24/7 accessible device

More than 16 million people in England and Wales risk dying from a cardiac arrest because they live farther than a 1km round trip from the nearest 24/7 defibrillator, according to exclusive research.

Analysis of publicly available defibrillators by the Heart Restart campaign found that in England and Wales alone, 35 million people – more than half the population – do not live within the recommended three- to five-minute brisk walk of a defibrillator. Of these, about half live more than a 1km round trip from a 24/7 accessible defibrillator.

There are more than 40,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests each year in the UK, but fewer than one in 10 people survive. However, early cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation can more than double the chance of survival.
